title: 14 October 2004: remembering Dattopant Thengadi
author: Editorial Desk
summary: Dattopant Thengadi passed away at Pune at the age of 83. What he left behind.
body:
*Photo: Dattopant Thengadi*

**Dattopant Thengadi** died on **14 October 2004** in Pune, at the age of 83. Every year, on this date, the karyakartas of the Bharatiya Mazdoor Sangh and of the organisations he founded remember him. This post looks at the day itself, at what contemporaries wrote about him, and at what he left behind.

## The last days

According to the report in *Organiser* of 31 October 2004, Thengadi died in a private nursing home in Pune on 14 October, after a fall at home. Wikipedia records the cause of death as a brain haemorrhage. His body was brought the next morning to the auditorium of the new Marathishala in Pune, where, as the same report says, thousands of people lined up for a last darshan. The funeral procession left at about four in the afternoon, passed through well-known parts of the city and reached Baikunthadham, where the last rites were performed. His nephew lit the pyre. The cremation was attended by the former Prime Minister Atal Bihari Vajpayee, the RSS Sarsanghchalak K. S. Sudarshan and Sarkaryavah Mohan Bhagwat, along with leaders of the organisations he had built, including the then BMS President Hasubhai Dave, the Swadeshi Jagaran Manch convenor Muralidhar Rao and the Bharatiya Kisan Sangh general secretary Baba Takwale. His ashes were immersed at Nashik, and two urns were taken to Delhi and Kanpur.

## The man

Thengadi was born on 10 November 1920 in Arvi, in the Wardha district of Maharashtra. He studied at Morris College and took a law degree from the Law College in Nagpur. Those who knew him describe someone who never sought recognition. He was a full-time RSS pracharak for most of his working life, served in the Rajya Sabha for two terms from 1964 to 1976, and held no property.

In 2003 he was offered a national civilian honour and declined it. A *Business Standard* report of February 2003 says that he wrote to the President that he would not be comfortable accepting it until the founders of the RSS movement, Dr Hedgewar and Guruji Golwalkar, were honoured with the Bharat Ratna. Other sources name the honour as the Padma Bhushan; in either case the main point is the same: he preferred that attention go to others.

After his death, **S. Gurumurthy** wrote a tribute that was titled, in effect, "a *tapasvi* dies, unnoticed." He observed that the man who built the BMS, the Kisan Sangh and the Swadeshi Jagaran Manch had himself remained little known, because he avoided publicity, rarely gave interviews or sat for photographs, and believed that people who build the nation should work rather than seek fame. Gurumurthy also noted that Thengadi lived simply, owned no property and never married, and that he was a scholar of economics, history, sociology and politics who wrote on a wide range of subjects in Hindi, English and Marathi.

## The legacy in numbers and institutions

The principal institutions linked to Thengadi are listed below.

- The **Bharatiya Mazdoor Sangh** (1955), which was founded on 23 July 1955, the birth anniversary of Lokmanya Tilak. It has since grown into a national trade union centre. In his tribute, Gurumurthy recorded that its membership passed 3.1 million by 1989 and was over eight million at the time of writing; these are figures he cited, and official verification exercises of the Government of India have separately placed BMS among the largest central trade unions.
- The **Bharatiya Kisan Sangh** (1979), the farmers' organisation.
- The **Swadeshi Jagaran Manch** (1991), set up when liberalisation began to change India's economy, to argue for an indigenous alternative.
- Other bodies in which he had a hand, including the **Akhil Bharatiya Vidyarthi Parishad**, the **Akhil Bharatiya Grahak Panchayat** for consumers, the **Samajik Samarasata Manch**, the **Akhil Bharatiya Adhivakta Parishad** and the **Bharatiya Vichara Kendra**.
- His writings. Titles associated with him include *The Third Way*, *Modernization without Westernization*, *Our National Renaissance*, *The Perspective*, and *Marx and Deen Dayal: Two Approaches*. The Dattopant Thengadi archive also lists *Labour Policy*, among other books, and a library of talks on subjects such as swadeshi and the WTO.

## How he is honoured

The BMS head office at 27 Deendayal Upadhyay Marg in New Delhi is named **Dattopant Thengadi Bhawan**. The Central Board for Workers' Education, the autonomous body under the Ministry of Labour and Employment that conducts the Workers' Education Scheme, now carries his name: it is called the **Dattopant Thengadi National Board for Workers' Education and Development**. According to its website, the Board offers training programmes for organised, unorganised and rural workers, gives grants to trade unions and other institutions for their own programmes, and works through fifty regional directorates. It is fitting that an institution whose work is the education of the worker should bear the name of a man who spent his life teaching workers to understand their own rights and duties.

## Why his method still matters

Thengadi's approach to the labour movement had a few steady features, and they are easy to recognise in the way the BMS functions even today.

1. **Independence from political parties.** He is said to have kept the union separate from party politics, and BMS to this day describes itself as a trade union and not a party wing.
2. **Responsive cooperation.** BMS cooperates with a government or an employer when workers' interests are served, and opposes when they are not. This is why it can both welcome a reform and protest against another on the same day.
3. **Constructive methods.** Firm demands, but a preference for representation, dialogue and, where necessary, peaceful agitation over disruption.
4. **Three interests in balance.** The nation, the industry and the worker, in that order of concern, with the consumer not forgotten.
5. **Dignity of the worker.** The idea that a worker is a builder of the nation and not merely a factor of production, which is also behind the BMS's observance of Vishwakarma Jayanti as its labour day.

## A question to ask

The anniversary is a moment for reflection rather than ritual. A karyakarta may ask three simple questions. Have I read at least one of Thengadi's writings in the past year? Is my union, in its daily work, following his idea of putting the nation, the industry and the worker together? And am I willing to work, as he did, without seeking credit?

On this day, the right question is not only "what did he build?" but "what are we building today?"
